title: Chapter 25 — The Greeting: Opening Without Triggering
intro: The first thirty seconds decide whether you get a conversation or a defensive shield. Step 1 of the 10 Steps — Engagement — is the most underestimated skill on the floor.

sections.title: The Wall Goes Up Immediately
sections.content:
The moment a customer walks through the door, they are already preparing to say 'just looking.' It is a reflex. They do not mean it — they are protecting themselves from being sold to before they are ready.

Your job in the first thirty seconds is not to sell. It is to be a human being. Make them feel welcome, not hunted.

The greeting that triggers the wall: 'Hi, can I help you find something today?' That sounds helpful. But the customer hears: 'I am about to sell you something.' And they shut down.

The greeting that opens the conversation: 'Hey, welcome in. Take your time — I am right here if you have any questions.' That sounds like zero pressure. Which is exactly what it is.

sections.title: Engagement Is Not Selling
sections.content:
Step 1 of the 10 Steps is Engagement. Engagement does not mean pitching. It means making contact.

The goal of the greeting is simple: start a conversation. Not a presentation. Not a product tour. A conversation.

The best openers are casual, warm, and pressure-free. Comment on the weather. Ask if they found the store easily. Compliment something genuine. Let the conversation develop naturally.

Once they are talking — actually talking, not just responding with one-word answers — you have engagement. Now you can transition to Step 2: Rapport.

sections.title: Read the Customer
sections.content:
Not every customer wants the same greeting. Some want to chat. Some want to be left alone for a few minutes. Some are in a hurry. Some are overwhelmed.

The skill is reading the room. A couple browsing slowly and talking to each other? Give them space. A person walking in with purpose and looking around? Approach quickly — they know what they want and they need help finding it. A family with kids? Acknowledge everyone, not just the adults.

Engagement is not one-size-fits-all. The best greeting is the one that matches the customer standing in front of you.

sections.title: The 'Just Looking' Recovery
sections.content:
When a customer says 'just looking,' most salespeople walk away. That is the wrong move.

Instead, treat it as the beginning — not the end. 'No problem at all. Take your time. If you do not mind me asking, what brought you in today?'

That question shifts the dynamic. It is not pushy. It is curious. And more often than not, the customer starts talking. 'Well, our fridge died last week' or 'we are renovating our kitchen.' Now you have context. Now you can help.

The key is to accept their boundary and then gently reopen the door. Not every customer will let you in. But many will — if the approach feels respectful.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating the greeting, ask:

Does the salesperson approach with warmth or with a sales pitch?
Do they adapt their greeting to the customer's energy and body language?
Can they recover from 'just looking' without being pushy?
Do they transition naturally from engagement to rapport — or jump straight to product?
Does the customer look comfortable or defensive after the greeting?

The first thirty seconds set the tone for the entire sale. Get them right and everything else flows more naturally.
